title: The Taiping Rebellion: China's Deadliest Civil War

cards.h: A civil war that killed more than the first World War
cards.b:
Between 1850 and 1864 a movement called the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom fought the Qing dynasty across southern and central China. Estimates of the dead run from about 20 million to more than 30 million, which makes it one of the deadliest wars in history.

It is less well known than the Opium Wars, but it shaped China's future. The Qing survived, but only by relying on new armies, and the state was weakened for decades.

cards.h: A failed scholar with a vision
cards.b:
Hong Xiuquan, born in 1814, was a Hakka scholar from Guangdong who failed the civil service exams several times. After a sickness in 1837 he claimed that he had visions of a heavenly father and of Jesus, whom he called his elder brother.

He spent years teaching his ideas, which mixed Christian scripture, Chinese tradition and his own revelations. Many poor and dispossessed people in Guangxi were drawn to his message.

In 1851 Hong and his followers declared the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom. They attacked and took Nanjing in 1853, which they renamed Tianjing, the Heavenly Capital. They set up a new state with its own calendar, land rules and religious practice.

The Taiping banned foot-binding and opium, and they promised land to peasants. These policies appealed to many people, but the movement also became brutal and divided by infighting.

cards.h: Jonathan Spence and God's Chinese Son
cards.b:
Jonathan Spence, God's Chinese Son (1996)

Spence tells the story of Hong Xiuquan with great skill. He shows how Hong's visions, his conflicts with his followers and his failures shaped the rebellion.

The book is a good starting point, though it depends on the surviving Taiping texts, which are partial and shaped by propaganda.
The movement lasted about fourteen years. In that time it held a large region, but the Qing fought back and regained control.

cards.h: Civil war and the leadership crisis
cards.b:
In 1856 a violent power struggle broke out among the Taiping leaders. Thousands were killed, and the movement lost its best commanders. Hong stayed isolated in Nanjing, and his authority was no longer secure.

The crisis weakened the Taiping at the very moment that the Qing began to organise new armies. The rebels never fully recovered the momentum of their early years.

The Qing relied on local militias led by scholars such as Zeng Guofan. He raised the Xiang Army from his home province of Hunan. The state also hired foreign soldiers, including the Ever Victorious Army led by Frederick Townsend Ward and later Charles Gordon.

These armies fought the Taiping for years. Zeng Guofan's success showed that the Qing could still produce talented generals, but it also gave local leaders more power.

Hong is often described in the West as a Chinese Christian who tried to bring Christianity to China. This picture made the rebellion seem like a religious crusade.

Historians argue that Hong's religion was heavily reshaped by his visions and his own reading of the Bible. Western missionaries who met him were often shocked by his views. His movement was religious, but it was also political and social.

cards.h: Hong's death and the fall of Nanjing
cards.b:
Hong Xiuquan died in June 1864, shortly before the Qing forces broke into Nanjing. Accounts say he died of illness or by taking poison. The city was taken in July 1864 and was heavily destroyed.

The fall of Nanjing ended the Taiping state. The killings and destruction in the capital and nearby towns were huge, and they added to the death toll of the war.

cards.h: A war that shaped modern China
cards.b:
The Taiping Rebellion left deep scars. Large areas of the Yangtze valley were devastated, and population and farming took decades to recover. The war also showed how fragile the Qing was, and it weakened the dynasty in the decades that followed.

Chinese historians have often seen the Taiping as a precursor to the revolution of the 1900s. Historians argue about how far the movement really anticipated modern ideas.

The Taiping war overlapped with the 1857 revolt in India. The British had been fighting the Second Opium War in China, and troops that were headed to China were diverted to India when the revolt broke out.

Lord Elgin, the British envoy in China, saw his forces redirected to the subcontinent. Two great revolts and two imperial wars were running at once, with British power stretched across Asia.

Five things to remember
  1. Hong Xiuquan led the Taiping movement from 1851.
  2. Nanjing was taken in 1853 and retaken by the Qing in 1864.
  3. Zeng Guofan built a new army in Hunan.
  4. The war killed millions and weakened the Qing.
  5. Western missionaries rejected Hong's teachings.
Think about it
  • Why did the Qing need foreign help to beat a rebellion?
  • Was the Taiping a religious movement, a social revolt or a political one?
